summary: When a DNS query is redirected by a CNAME or DNAME, the answer can involve several lookup rounds. This RFC clarifies how the response code (RCODE) and status bits in the final answer relate to the first lookup and to the later ones. It updates RFC 1035, RFC 2308 and RFC 2672.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how a DNS response reports results when a name redirects a query to another name. The response code comes from the final lookup, while the status bits follow their defined rules.

subtitle: Clarifying DNS response codes and status bits after name redirection.

tldr.problem: A redirected DNS lookup can involve several query cycles, leaving unclear which cycle determines the response code and status bits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that the final RCODE reflects the final query cycle, while restating the existing rules for the Authoritative Answer and Authentic Data bits.
tldr.outcome: It clarifies DNS behavior for chains of redirections and updates RFCs 1035, 2308, and 2672.

today: RFC 6604 is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 1035, RFC 2308, and RFC 2672. It clarifies how DNS response fields apply to redirected queries.

sections.title: Queries That Follow Name Redirections
sections.content:
DNS records such as CNAME and DNAME can redirect a query to another name. If another redirection is found, the lookup may continue through a chain until it reaches a non-redirection name or an error. RFC 6604 calls these redirection records xNAME records.

A DNS response includes an RCODE and status bits. This RFC clarifies how those fields apply when a lookup follows an xNAME chain.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS lookup may be sent from one name to another and then redirected again. This RFC explains which result the final response should report.

sections.title: The Final Response Code
sections.content: When a query follows an xNAME chain, each earlier query cycle must have succeeded for the redirection to continue. The RCODE in the final response MUST be based on the final query cycle. If that cycle ends in an error, the response uses that error code; if it ends without error, the RCODE is zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The final response code reports the result of the last lookup in the chain. Earlier successful redirections do not determine that code.

sections.title: The AA and AD Status Bits
sections.content:
The Authoritative Answer (AA) bit indicates whether the server providing the answer with the first owner name in the answer section is authoritative for its zone. The RFC restates this existing rule; authority may differ among answers in a chain.

The Authentic Data (AD) bit indicates that a DNSSEC-enabled server believes all records in the answer and authority sections are authentic. RFC 6604 also restates this existing rule.
sections.plainLanguage: AA reports authority for the first answer name. AD indicates that the DNSSEC-enabled server considers all records in the answer and authority sections authentic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that DNSSEC does not protect the AA bit and does not generally protect the AD bit or RCODE in a response. Securing those fields requires secure communication between the querying resolver and server, such as through TSIG or SIG(0). The memo describes conditions under which a querier can validate AD and an NXDOMAIN RCODE using DNSSEC data.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC does not generally protect every response-header field. The RFC says secure communication between the resolver and server may be needed to protect them.
